candidate.answerReason: Substituting the line into the ellipse gives a genuine quadratic whose discriminant is \(16m^2-12\). Exactly one intersection requires this discriminant to be zero.

methods.label: Translate one intersection into one real root
methods.explanation:
Substituting the line equation into the ellipse removes \(y\), allowing us to count intersections by counting possible \(x\)-coordinates. We obtain
\[
x^2+4(mx+1)^2=1,
\]
which expands to
\[
(1+4m^2)x^2+8mx+3=0.
\]
For every real \(m\), the leading coefficient \(1+4m^2\) is positive, so this is always a quadratic. Each real root determines exactly one intersection through \(y=mx+1\), and every intersection gives such a root.

A quadratic has exactly one distinct real root when its discriminant is zero. Here the discriminant is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta&=(8m)^2-4(1+4m^2)(3)\\
&=16m^2-12.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
16m^2-12=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
m^2=\frac34.
\]
Conversely, either real slope with this square makes the discriminant zero while the leading coefficient remains nonzero, so it does give exactly one intersection. Therefore \(m^2=\frac34\), choice C.
methods.levelReason: Substitution and the quadratic discriminant give a complete high-school algebra solution without needing further ellipse properties.

review.mathematicalCheck: Substitution gives (1+4m²)x²+8mx+3=0, whose leading coefficient never vanishes. Intersections correspond bijectively to real roots, so discriminant 16m²-12=0 is necessary and sufficient, yielding m²=3/4.
